claim: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer deaths in both men and women in the United States and worldwide.
source: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer deaths in both men and women in the United States and worldwide (Siegel et al., 2020; Bray et al., 2018; Torre et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Siegel et al., 2020; Bray et al., 2018; Torre et al., 2016)

claim: Global cancer statistics estimated 1,761,007 deaths due to lung cancer in 2018, contributing to about 20% of all cancer deaths.
source: Global cancer statistics estimated 1,761,007 deaths due to lung cancer in 2018, contributing to about 20% of all cancer deaths (Bray et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Bray et al., 2018)

claim: In 2020, there were an estimated 228,820 newly diagnosed lung cancer cases and 135,720 lung cancer deaths in the United States alone.
source: In 2020, there were an estimated 228,820 newly diagnosed lung cancer cases and 135,720 lung cancer deaths in the United States alone (Siegel et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Siegel et al., 2020)

claim: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) accounts for approximately 85% of lung cancer cases.
source: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) accounts for approximately 85% of lung cancer cases and includes the major subtypes: lung adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and large cell carcinoma (Herbst et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Herbst et al., 2018)

claim: NSCLC includes the major subtypes: lung adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and large cell carcinoma.
source: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) accounts for approximately 85% of lung cancer cases and includes the major subtypes: lung adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and large cell carcinoma (Herbst et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Herbst et al., 2018)

claim: Small-molecule inhibitors targeted at driver gain-of-function gene mutations have achieved improved clinical outcomes over conventional cytotoxic therapy.
source: While small-molecule inhibitors targeted at driver gain-of-function gene mutations have achieved improved clinical outcomes over conventional cytotoxic therapy, they are currently available for only a subset of patients with lung cancer harboring specific mutations such as EGFR and ALK mutations (Howlader et al., 2020; Koivunen et al., 2008; Paez et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Howlader et al., 2020; Koivunen et al., 2008; Paez et al., 2004)

claim: Targeted small-molecule inhibitors are currently available for only a subset of patients with lung cancer harboring specific mutations such as EGFR and ALK mutations.
source: While small-molecule inhibitors targeted at driver gain-of-function gene mutations have achieved improved clinical outcomes over conventional cytotoxic therapy, they are currently available for only a subset of patients with lung cancer harboring specific mutations such as EGFR and ALK mutations (Howlader et al., 2020; Koivunen et al., 2008; Paez et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Howlader et al., 2020; Koivunen et al., 2008; Paez et al., 2004)

claim: Immune checkpoint inhibitors blocking the PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint pathway offer durable tumor responses to only a small population of patients generally with high tumor PD-L1 expression and/or high tumor mutational burden.
source: Cancer immunotherapy has emerged as one of the newest treatment options for NSCLC; however, the recent use of immune checkpoint inhibitors, such as those blocking the PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint pathway, offer durable tumor responses to only a small population of patients generally with high tumor PD-L1 expression and/or high tumor mutational burden (Herbst et al., 2018; Reck et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Herbst et al., 2018; Reck et al., 2016)

claim: Effective treatments for the majority of lung cancer patients remain lacking.
source: Therefore, effective treatments for the majority of lung cancer patients remain lacking.
evidence: Inferred from the limited efficacy of current therapies described in the preceding text

claim: Comprehensive genomic profiling has revealed the genetic landscape of lung cancer.
source: Comprehensive genomic profiling has revealed the genetic landscape of lung cancer (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2014; Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2012; Ding et al., 2008), identifying inactivating somatic STK11 gene mutations as a common event in NSCLC.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2014; Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2012; Ding et al., 2008)

claim: Inactivating somatic STK11 gene mutations are a common event in NSCLC.
source: Comprehensive genomic profiling has revealed the genetic landscape of lung cancer (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2014; Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2012; Ding et al., 2008), identifying inactivating somatic STK11 gene mutations as a common event in NSCLC.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2014; Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2012; Ding et al., 2008)

claim: Somatic STK11 mutations arise preferentially in lung adenocarcinoma where they have been detected in up to 30% of cases.
source: Somatic STK11 mutations arise preferentially in lung adenocarcinoma where they have been detected in up to 30% of cases (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2014; Ding et al., 2008; Matsumoto et al., 2007; Sanchez-Cespedes et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2014; Ding et al., 2008; Matsumoto et al., 2007; Sanchez-Cespedes et al., 2002)

claim: STK11 can be inactivated by epigenetic silencing, post-translational modifications, or alterations in its interacting proteins.
source: In addition to gene mutations, STK11 can be inactivated by epigenetic silencing, post-translational modifications, or alterations in its interacting proteins (Boudeau et al., 2003; Esteller et al., 2000; Zheng et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Boudeau et al., 2003; Esteller et al., 2000; Zheng et al., 2009)

claim: The STK11 gene encodes a serine-threonine kinase, commonly known as liver kinase B1 (LKB1).
source: The STK11 gene encodes a serine-threonine kinase, commonly known as liver kinase B1 (LKB1).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about the STK11 gene product

claim: Lung cancer with LKB1 deficiency exhibits resistance to chemotherapy, targeted therapeutics and especially to immune checkpoint inhibitors in preclinical models and/or human patients.
source: Lung cancer with LKB1 deficiency exhibits resistance to chemotherapy, targeted therapeutics and especially to immune checkpoint inhibitors in preclinical models and/or human patients (Chen et al., 2012; Carretero et al., 2010; Han et al., 2014; Skoulidis et al., 2018; Schabath et al., 2016; Rizvi et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Chen et al., 2012; Carretero et al., 2010; Han et al., 2014; Skoulidis et al., 2018; Schabath et al., 2016; Rizvi et al., 2018)

claim: The absence of targeted therapies and the lack of benefits of immune checkpoint inhibitors for LKB1-deficient lung cancer require an urgent search for new therapeutic strategies.
source: Therefore, the absence of targeted therapies and the lack of benefits of immune checkpoint inhibitors for this common aggressive lung cancer subtype require an urgent search for new therapeutic strategies.
evidence: Inferred from the resistance to current therapies described in the preceding text

claim: STK11 was first identified as the cancer susceptibility locus for familial Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS).
source: STK11 was first identified as the cancer susceptibility locus for familial Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS), which is characterized by mucocutaneous pigmentation and gastrointestinal hamartoma with an increased cancer risk (Hemminki et al., 1998; Giardiello et al., 1987).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Hemminki et al., 1998; Giardiello et al., 1987)

claim: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is characterized by mucocutaneous pigmentation and gastrointestinal hamartoma with an increased cancer risk.
source: STK11 was first identified as the cancer susceptibility locus for familial Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS), which is characterized by mucocutaneous pigmentation and gastrointestinal hamartoma with an increased cancer risk (Hemminki et al., 1998; Giardiello et al., 1987).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Hemminki et al., 1998; Giardiello et al., 1987)

claim: Somatic inactivation of LKB1 has been observed in a variety of human cancers besides lung cancer.
source: Somatic inactivation of LKB1 has now been observed in a variety of human cancers besides lung cancer.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about LKB1 mutations in cancer

claim: LKB1 loss has been shown to promote cancer progression and increase metastatic potential in genetically engineered mouse models of lung cancer, melanoma, pancreatic cancer, and endometrial cancer.
source: Importantly, LKB1 loss has been shown to promote cancer progression and increase metastatic potential in the genetically engineered mouse models of lung cancer, melanoma, pancreatic cancer, and endometrial cancer (Hermanova et al., 2020; Ji et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2012; Peña et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Hermanova et al., 2020; Ji et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2012; Peña et al., 2015)

claim: STK11 mutations are associated with the suppressive immune milieu of the lung tumor microenvironment.
source: Also, STK11 mutations are associated with the suppressive immune milieu of the lung tumor microenvironment (Schabath et al., 2016; Koyama et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Schabath et al., 2016; Koyama et al., 2016)

claim: STK11 is a bona fide tumor suppressor gene.
source: Thus, STK11 is a bona fide tumor suppressor gene.
evidence: Inferred from the evidence of LKB1 loss promoting cancer progression and metastasis described in the preceding text

claim: The LKB1 kinase is essential for the activation of 14 downstream AMPK family members, such as AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) and salt-inducible kinases (SIKs).
source: The LKB1 kinase is essential for the activation of 14 downstream AMPK family members, such as AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) and salt-inducible kinases (SIKs) (Alessi et al., 2006; Shackelford and Shaw, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Alessi et al., 2006; Shackelford and Shaw, 2009)

claim: LKB1 regulates multiple signaling pathways through its various substrates and plays critical roles in regulating cell polarity, metabolism, and growth.
source: Therefore, LKB1 regulates multiple signaling pathways through its various substrates and plays critical roles in regulating cell polarity, metabolism, and growth (Alessi et al., 2006; Shackelford and Shaw, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Alessi et al., 2006; Shackelford and Shaw, 2009)

claim: Loss of AMPK was found to reduce the growth of murine oncogenic Kras G12D-driven lung cancer.
source: However, unlike loss of LKB1, loss of AMPK was found to reduce the growth of murine oncogenic Kras G12D-driven lung cancer (Eichner et al., 2019), indicating that AMPK does not mediate LKB1's tumor suppression function.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Eichner et al., 2019)

claim: AMPK does not mediate LKB1's tumor suppression function.
source: However, unlike loss of LKB1, loss of AMPK was found to reduce the growth of murine oncogenic Kras G12D-driven lung cancer (Eichner et al., 2019), indicating that AMPK does not mediate LKB1's tumor suppression function.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that AMPK loss reduces tumor growth, opposite to LKB1 loss

claim: Multiple cAMP/CREB-regulated targets, such as LINC00473, INSL4, NR4A1-3, and PTGS2, were highly expressed in human LKB1-null lung cancer cell lines and primary tumors.
source: To identify key signaling pathway(s) impacted by LKB1 inactivation in lung cancer, we previously performed an unbiased global gene expression profiling analysis and discovered that multiple cAMP/CREB-regulated targets, such as LINC00473, INSL4, NR4A1-3, and PTGS2, were highly expressed in human LKB1-null lung cancer cell lines and primary tumors (Yang et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to the authors' previous publications (Yang et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2016)

claim: The induction of cAMP/CREB-mediated targets was linked with aberrant hyper-activation of the CRTC family in the context of LKB1 deficiency.
source: The induction of these cAMP/CREB-mediated targets was linked with aberrant hyper-activation of the CRTC (CREB-regulated transcription co-activator) family in the context of LKB1 deficiency (Yang et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to the authors' previous publications (Yang et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2016)

claim: The top 17 compounds that positively correlated with the LKB1-null gene signature from the Broad Institute Connectivity Map were all compounds directly associated with CRTC activation.
source: In addition, we previously generated an LKB1-null gene signature from 53 lung cancer cell lines to screen the Broad Institute Connectivity Map (CMAP) drug response database and the top 17 compounds that positively correlated with the LKB1-null gene signature were all compounds directly associated with CRTC activation (Cao et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to the authors' previous publication (Cao et al., 2015)

claim: The CRTC family consists of three members, CRTC1, CRTC2, and CRTC3.
source: The CRTC family consists of three members, CRTC1, CRTC2, and CRTC3, which play important roles in metabolism, aging, and cancer (Altarejos and Montminy, 2011; Iourgenko et al., 2003; Conkright et al., 2003; Tonon et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Altarejos and Montminy, 2011; Iourgenko et al., 2003; Conkright et al., 2003; Tonon et al., 2003)

claim: CRTC proteins play important roles in metabolism, aging, and cancer.
source: The CRTC family consists of three members, CRTC1, CRTC2, and CRTC3, which play important roles in metabolism, aging, and cancer (Altarejos and Montminy, 2011; Iourgenko et al., 2003; Conkright et al., 2003; Tonon et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Altarejos and Montminy, 2011; Iourgenko et al., 2003; Conkright et al., 2003; Tonon et al., 2003)

claim: CRTC proteins function as latent transcriptional co-activators and are normally sequestered in the cytoplasm.
source: These three CRTC proteins function as latent transcriptional co-activators and are normally sequestered in the cytoplasm.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about CRTC protein function

claim: In response to cAMP and/or calcium signals, the family of three salt-inducible kinases (SIK1, 2, 3) are inactivated and/or phosphatases become activated, leading to CRTC dephosphorylation.
source: In response to cAMP and/or calcium signals, the family of three salt-inducible kinases (SIK1, 2, 3) are inactivated and/or phosphatases become activated, leading to CRTC dephosphorylation.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about CRTC regulation

claim: Dephosphorylated CRTCs translocate to the nucleus and interact with the transcription factor CREB, activating CRE-containing promoters.
source: Dephosphorylated CRTCs subsequently translocate to the nucleus and interact with the transcription factor CREB, activating CRE (cAMP-responsive element)-containing promoters.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about CRTC function

claim: LKB1 deficiency impairs SIKs to phosphorylate CRTCs and consequently leads to an elevated level of unphosphorylated CRTCs, resulting in CRTC nuclear translocation and activation of CREB-mediated transcription.
source: Since SIKs are dependent on LKB1 for its kinase activity, LKB1 deficiency impairs SIKs to phosphorylate CRTCs and consequently leads to an elevated level of unphosphorylated CRTCs, resulting in CRTC nuclear translocation and activation of CREB-mediated transcription.
evidence: Inferred from the established knowledge that SIKs require LKB1 for activity and that SIKs phosphorylate CRTCs

claim: Knock-outs of SIK1 and SIK3, but not of other AMPK family members, increased tumor growth in a mouse model of oncogenic KRAS-driven lung adenocarcinoma.
source: This notion is further supported by recent CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing studies revealing that knock-outs of SIK1 and SIK3, but not of other AMPK family members, increased tumor growth in a mouse model of oncogenic KRAS-driven lung adenocarcinoma (Hollstein et al., 2019; Murray et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Hollstein et al., 2019; Murray et al., 2019)

claim: SIKs mediate the major tumor suppressive effects of LKB1 in NSCLC.
source: Therefore, SIKs mediate the major tumor suppressive effects of LKB1 in NSCLC.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that SIK1 and SIK3 knockouts increase tumor growth

claim: CRTC2 was reported to promote tumor growth in LKB1-deficient NSCLC.
source: Moreover, CRTC2 was reported to promote tumor growth in LKB1-deficient NSCLC (Rodón et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Rodón et al., 2019)

claim: The three CRTC genes were all expressed at varying levels in lung cancer cells, with CRTC2 and CRTC3 having higher relative expression than CRTC1 at the transcript level.
source: We observed that the three CRTC genes were all expressed at varying levels, with CRTC2 and CRTC3 having higher relative expression than CRTC1 at the transcript level (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1A

claim: CRTC protein levels did not tightly correlate with their RNA transcript levels.
source: Also, there were variable CRTC protein levels in all the cell lines examined and protein levels did not tightly correlate with their RNA transcript levels (Figure 1B), suggesting potential post-transcriptional regulation.
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1B

claim: CRTC1 and CRTC2 exhibited predominantly faster migrating bands in all six LKB1-null cancer cells, consistent with enrichment of dephosphorylated forms in the setting of LKB1 deficiency.
source: CRTC1 and CRTC2 exhibited predominantly faster migrating bands in all six LKB1-null cancer cells, consistent with enrichment of dephosphorylated forms in the setting of LKB1 deficiency.
evidence: Inferred from the western blot migration patterns and established knowledge that dephosphorylated proteins migrate faster

claim: The mobility of CRTC3 appeared relatively unchanged in 4/6 LKB1-null cancer cell lines, suggesting a distinct pattern of post-translational regulation.
source: However, the mobility of CRTC3 appeared relatively unchanged in 4/6 LKB1-null cancer cell lines, suggesting a distinct pattern of post-translational regulation.
evidence: Inferred from the western blot migration patterns

claim: Endogenous CRTC1, CRTC2, and CRTC3 proteins showed slow migration patterns in LKB1-expressing lung cancer cells (H322).
source: As shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, endogenous CRTC1, CRTC2, and CRTC3 proteins showed slow migration patterns in LKB1-expressing lung cancer cells (H322).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: Endogenous CRTCs are predominantly phosphorylated in LKB1-expressing cells and dephosphorylated in LKB1-null cells.
source: These data demonstrate that endogenous CRTCs are predominantly phosphorylated in LKB1-expressing cells and dephosphorylated in LKB1-null cells.
evidence: Inferred from the phosphatase treatment and migration pattern data

claim: CRTC proteins were predominantly detected as dephosphorylated, nuclear forms in LKB1-null cells and phosphorylated, cytoplasmic forms in LKB1-expressing cells.
source: Further immunoblot analysis of the nuclear and cytoplasmic fractions revealed that the CRTC proteins were predominantly detected as dephosphorylated, nuclear forms in LKB1-null cells and phosphorylated, cytoplasmic forms in LKB1-expressing cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: Reintroduction of LKB1 to LKB1-null A549 cells led to an increase in the levels of phosphorylated CRTCs, which correlated with a decrease in nuclear CRTCs and an increase in cytoplasmic CRTCs.
source: Reintroduction of LKB1 to LKB1-null A549 cells led to an increase in the levels of phosphorylated CRTCs, which correlated with a decrease in nuclear CRTCs and an increase in cytoplasmic CRTCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by LKB1 reintroduction experiment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: Individual CRTC knockout cells showed a reduction in expression of several CREB-mediated target genes, such as PDE4D, INSL4, LINC00473, and NR4A2, but not to the extent of their endogenous levels in LKB1-wt lung cancer H522 cells.
source: These individual CRTC knockout cells showed a reduction in expression of several CREB-mediated target genes, such as PDE4D, INSL4, LINC00473, and NR4A2, but not to the extent of their endogenous levels in LKB1-wt lung cancer H522 cells, as assayed by western blotting or RT-qPCR assays (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by western blot and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2A,B

claim: Knockout of each individual CRTC gene had only a mild effect on the numbers of viable cells, apoptotic cells, and colonies grown in soft agar.
source: We observed that knockout of each individual CRTC gene had only a mild effect on the numbers of viable cells, apoptotic cells, and colonies grown in soft agar (Figure 2C,D,E).
evidence: Supported by cell viability, apoptosis, and soft agar assay data shown in Figure 2C,D,E

claim: The CRTC family members may be functionally redundant in regulating lung cancer cell proliferation, survival, and anchorage-independent growth.
source: These data indicate that the CRTC family members may be functionally redundant in regulating lung cancer cell proliferation, survival, and anchorage-independent growth.
evidence: Inferred from the mild effects of individual CRTC knockouts

claim: The CRTC1-CBD-nls-GFP protein was predominantly localized in the nuclear compartment, while the control GFP showed diffuse cytoplasmic and nuclear signals.
source: We infected human LKB1-null lung cancer A549 cells with the CRTC1-CBD-nls-GFP or GFP (control) retroviruses and observed that CRTC1-CBD-nls-GFP was predominantly localized in the nuclear compartment, while the control GFP showed diffuse cytoplasmic and nuclear signals (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3B

claim: The CRTC1-CBD-nls-GFP chimeric protein showed an expected size of ~33 kDa.
source: The CRTC1-CBD-nls-GFP chimeric protein showed an expected size of ~33 kDa (Figure 3C) and suppressed the ability of the three CRTC co-activators to activate the CREB-dependent transcription in cAMP response element (CRE)-containing promoter luciferase reporter assays (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3C

claim: The CRTC1-CBD-nls-GFP chimeric protein suppressed the ability of the three CRTC co-activators to activate the CREB-dependent transcription in CRE-containing promoter luciferase reporter assays.
source: The CRTC1-CBD-nls-GFP chimeric protein showed an expected size of ~33 kDa (Figure 3C) and suppressed the ability of the three CRTC co-activators to activate the CREB-dependent transcription in cAMP response element (CRE)-containing promoter luciferase reporter assays (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 3D

claim: The CRTC1-CBD-nls-GFP chimeric protein functions as a dominant negative mutant for CRTC (dnCRTC), capable of blocking all three CRTCs to co-activate CREB-mediated transcription.
source: Therefore, the CRTC1-CBD-nls-GFP chimeric protein functions as a dominant negative mutant for CRTC (dnCRTC), capable of blocking all three CRTCs to co-activate CREB-mediated transcription.
evidence: Inferred from the luciferase reporter assay results showing suppression of CRTC-mediated transcription

claim: dnCRTC interacts with CREB in the chromatin complex.
source: Using chromatins prepared from dnCRTC- and control GFP-expressing A549 cells after cross-linking, we performed chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assay of dnCRTC or GFP using GFP-trap that consists of anti-GFP VHH nanobodies coupled to agarose beads (ChromoTek) or uncoupled agarose beads as negative control. Western blotting detected CREB in the dnCRTC-ChIP complex, but not in the control GFP ChIP complex (Figure 3E), demonstrating a physical association of dnCRTC and CREB.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-western blot data shown in Figure 3E

claim: The DNA sequences spanning the CRE regions within the promoters of LINC00473 and NR4A2 were significantly enriched in the dnCRTC ChIP complex.
source: We also observed that the DNA sequences spanning the CRE regions within the promoters of LINC00473 and NR4A2, two genes known to be upregulated by CRTC-CREB activation due to LKB1 deficiency, were significantly enriched in the dnCRTC ChIP complex, but not in the control GFP ChIP complex by RT-qPCR assays (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3F

claim: The enrichment of CRTCs on CRE-containing promoters (LINC00473 and NR4A2) was significantly reduced by dnCRTC expression.
source: Moreover, ChIP analysis using three CRTC antibodies showed that the enrichment of CRTCs on CRE-containing promotors (LINC00473 and NR4A2) was significantly reduced (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3G

claim: The dnCRTC mutant physically associates with CREB on the CRE-containing gene promoters and blocks the recruitment of endogenous CRTC proteins.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that the dnCRTC (CRTC1-CBD-nls-GFP) mutant physically associates with CREB on the CRE-containing gene promoters and blocks the recruitment of endogenous CRTC proteins, thus acting as a pan-inhibitor for all three CRTCs in co-activating CREB-mediated transcription.
evidence: Inferred from the ChIP data showing dnCRTC binding to CREB and reduced endogenous CRTC recruitment

claim: A total of 274 dnCRTC-regulated differentially expressed genes (dnCRTC-DEGs) were identified, including 114 upregulated and 160 downregulated genes.
source: Using cut-off criteria of an absolute fold-change >= 2.0 and FDR p<0.05, we identified a total of 274 dnCRTC-regulated differentially expressed genes (dnCRTC-DEGs), including 114 upregulated and 160 downregulated genes (Supplementary file 1a); the heatmap and volcano plot were shown in Figure 4B,C.
evidence: Supported by gene expression profiling data shown in Figure 4B,C and Supplementary file 1a

claim: dnCRTC expression reduced the expression levels of multiple genes including INSL4, CPS1, NR4A2, LINC00473, NR4A1, PTGS2, SIK1, and PDE4D.
source: Since CRTCs are transcriptional co-activators, we next focused on the top downregulated dnCRTC-DEGs for the validation of the microarray results and confirmed that dnCRTC expression reduced the expression levels of multiple genes by RT-qPCR analysis (Figure 4D). These genes include known LKB1 target genes, such as INSL4, CPS1, NR4A2, LINC00473, NR4A1, PTGS2, SIK1, and PDE4D.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR validation data shown in Figure 4D

claim: The majority of the dnCRTC-regulated gene candidates tested were downregulated in a second LKB1-null cancer cell line H157, but were not affected in 2 LKB1-expressing cell lines (H322 and H522).
source: We further showed that the majority of the dnCRTC-regulated gene candidates tested were downregulated in a second LKB1-null cancer cell line H157, but were not affected in 2 LKB1-expressing cell lines (H322 and H522) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: LKB1 knockout in LKB1-expressing cancer cells (H322) led to a significant upregulation of multiple target genes.
source: LKB1 knockout in LKB1-expressing cancer cells (H322) led to a significant upregulation of multiple target genes, although not to the extent that was observed in the naturally occurring human LKB1-null lung cancer cells (A549) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: The expression levels of many dnCRTC-regulated genes were significantly higher in human TCGA lung cancers harboring LKB1 mutations, particularly in lung adenocarcinomas.
source: Finally, the expression levels of many dnCRTC-regulated genes were significantly higher in human TCGA lung cancers harboring LKB1 mutations, particularly in lung adenocarcinomas (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2014; Ding et al., 2008; Gao et al., 2013; Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3

claim: CREB and cAMP are upstream regulators of gene expression changes observed in dnCRTC-expressing vs control A549 cells.
source: Ingenuity Pathway analysis revealed that CREB and cAMP are upstream regulators of gene expression changes observed in dnCRTC-expressing vs control A549 cells (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by Ingenuity Pathway Analysis shown in Figure 4E

claim: 169 of 274 (~61.7%) dnCRTC-DEGs contain predicted or experimentally verified CRE sites.
source: Moreover, we analyzed the dnCRTC-DEGs for predicted CRE sites on their promoters (−3 kb to 300 bp from transcription start site) using the CREB Target Gene Database (Zhang et al., 2005) and found that 169 of 274 (~61.7%) dnCRTC-DEGs contain predicted or experimentally verified CRE sites, which supports that dnCRTC affects a large set of CREB-regulated transcriptional loci (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: Supported by bioinformatics analysis using the CREB Target Gene Database

claim: The dnCRTC-DEGs exhibited significant enrichment in CREB and CRTC2 binding around their transcription start sites.
source: By incorporating a recently published ChIP-sequencing study that investigated the genome-wide binding profiles of CREB and CRTC2 in LKB1-null A549 cells (Rodón et al., 2019), we found that the dnCRTC-DEGs exhibited significant enrichment in CREB and CRTC2 binding around their transcription start sites (TSS), while the binding of CREB and CRTC2 was reduced upon reintroduction of LKB1 (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4F

claim: 97 of 274 (~35%) dnCRTC-DEGs have CREB-binding and CRTC2-binding peaks within −3 kb to 300 bp from TSS.
source: This analysis revealed 97 of 274 (~35%) dnCRTC-DEGs (60 down-regulated and 37 up-regulated) having CREB-binding and CRTC2-binding peaks within −3 kb to 300 bp from TSS; and 73 of 274 (~27%) dnCRTC-DEGs (45 down-regulated and 28 up-regulated) having both the CREB and CRTC2 binding peaks within −500 bp to 100 bp from TSS (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data analysis

claim: Several oncogenic gene signatures were found to be significantly altered with negative enrichment scores in dnCRTC-expressing cells.
source: To gain further insights into the biological impact of dnCRTC expression, we performed gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) of the transcriptomic data from dnCRTC-expressing vs control GFP-expressing A549 control cells using gene sets obtained from the Molecular Signatures Database. Several oncogenic gene signatures, such as Shh-regulated gene set, RB loss/E2F1-regulated gene set, NFE2L2-regulated gene set, PDGF-regulated gene set, KRAS-regulated gene set, were found to be significantly altered with negative enrichment scores (Supplementary file 1b), indicating that a majority of genes in these oncogenic gene sets were significantly under-expressed in dnCRTC-expressing cells.
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis

claim: A progressively reduced percentage of LKB1-null cells (A549 and H157) expressed dnCRTC, while the percent of the GFP-control cells remained stable.
source: We observed a progressively reduced percentage of LKB1-null cells (A549 and H157) that expressed dnCRTC, while the percent of the GFP-control cells remained stable (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by competition assay data shown in Figure 5A

claim: The percentage of LKB1-positive cells (H322 and H522) was not significantly affected by dnCRTC expression.
source: In contrast, the percentage of LKB1-positive cells (H322 and H522) was not significantly affected (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by competition assay data shown in Figure 5A

claim: dnCRTC expression has a negative effect on the proliferation of LKB1-null tumor cells, but not of LKB1-positive cells.
source: These results showed that dnCRTC expression has a negative effect on the proliferation of LKB1-null tumor cells, but not of LKB1-positive cells, indicating that CRTC activation is critical for LKB1-null cell growth.
evidence: Inferred from the competition assay results

claim: CRTC activation is critical for LKB1-null cell growth.
source: These results showed that dnCRTC expression has a negative effect on the proliferation of LKB1-null tumor cells, but not of LKB1-positive cells, indicating that CRTC activation is critical for LKB1-null cell growth.
evidence: Inferred from the selective effect of dnCRTC on LKB1-null cells

claim: dnCRTC expression induced a significant inhibition of cell growth in LKB1-null cells (A549 and H157), but not in LKB1-positive cells (H322 and H522).
source: We observed that dnCRTC expression induced a significant inhibition of cell growth in LKB1-null cells (A549 and H157), but not in LKB1-positive cells (H322 and H522) (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by cell growth assay data shown in Figure 5C

claim: dnCRTC expression did not affect cell proliferation in normal lung epithelial cells (BEAS-2B).
source: Importantly, dnCRTC expression did not affect cell proliferation in normal lung epithelial cells (BEAS-2B) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: Supported by cell proliferation data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C

claim: dnCRTC expression blocked colony-forming potential and anchorage-independent growth in LKB1-null cells (A549 and H157), but not in LKB1-positive cells (H322 and H522).
source: Moreover, colony formation and soft agar colony formation assay showed that dnCRTC expression blocked colony-forming potential and anchorage-independent growth in LKB1-null cells (A549 and H157), but not in LKB1-positive cells (H322 and H522) (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: Supported by colony formation and soft agar assay data shown in Figure 5D,E

claim: Expression of dnCRTC had a similar negative effect on the growth of a mouse lung squamous carcinoma cell line derived from a mouse model deficient of the tumor suppressors LKB1 and PTEN.
source: Expression of dnCRTC also had a similar negative effect on the growth of a mouse lung squamous carcinoma cell line, which was derived from a mouse model deficient of the tumor suppressors LKB1 and PTEN (Liu et al., 2019; Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-G).
evidence: Supported by cell growth data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-G

claim: LKB1-null NSCLC cells are specifically sensitive to dnCRTC expression and are highly dependent on the CRTC-CREB activation for growth.
source: These results demonstrated that LKB1-null NSCLC cells are specifically sensitive to dnCRTC expression; therefore, they are highly dependent on the CRTC-CREB activation for growth.
evidence: Inferred from the selective growth inhibition of LKB1-null cells by dnCRTC

claim: The dnCRTC cohorts had reduced growth of xenograft tumors compared to the GFP control cohorts, as demonstrated by the reduced tumor growth rate, size and weight.
source: The dnCRTC cohorts had reduced growth of xenograft tumors compared to the GFP control cohorts, as demonstrated by the reduced tumor growth rate, size and weight (Figure 6A–D,F–I).
evidence: Supported by subcutaneous xenograft data shown in Figure 6A–D,F–I

claim: Immunohistochemical analysis revealed a decreased number of Ki-67-positive proliferating cells in the dnCRTC-expressing xenograft tumors in comparison with the control GFP group.
source: Immunohistochemical analysis revealed a decreased number of Ki-67-positive proliferating cells in the dnCRTC-expressing xenograft tumors in comparison with the control GFP group (Figure 6E,J).
evidence: Supported by Ki-67 IHC data shown in Figure 6E,J

claim: Markedly reduced dnCRTC expression was observed in excised xenograft tumors when compared to dnCRTC-transduced cells at the time of the injection.
source: Since the tumor cells used in these xenograft assays were unsorted and not 100% transduced, we performed western blot analysis on the excised xenograft tumors and observed markedly reduced dnCRTC expression when compared to dnCRTC-transduced cells at the time of the injection.
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis of xenograft tumors shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: The residual small xenograft tumors in the dnCRTC group were likely derived from cells with low or no dnCRTC expression.
source: These results indicate that the residual small xenograft tumors in the dnCRTC group were likely derived from cells with low or no dnCRTC expression, further supporting the tumor inhibitory effect of dnCRTC expression on the growth of LKB1-null lung cancers.
evidence: Inferred from the reduced dnCRTC expression in xenograft tumors

claim: Mice injected with dnCRTC-expressing A549-luc or H157-luc cells had reduced tumor burden, a decreased number of surface tumor nodules and smaller tumor areas in the lung compared to mice with their control GFP counterparts.
source: We observed that mice injected with dnCRTC-expressing A549-luc or H157-luc cells, compared to mice with their control GFP counterparts, had reduced tumor burden, a decreased number of surface tumor nodules and smaller tumor areas in the lung, as assessed by bioluminescent imaging (Figure 7A,D), fluorescence imaging (Figure 7B,E), and H and E staining of lung sections (Figure 7C,F).
evidence: Supported by orthotopic xenograft data shown in Figure 7A-F

claim: Expression of dnCRTC blocked lung cancer growth and colonization in vivo.
source: Taken together, these data showed that expression of dnCRTC blocked lung cancer growth and colonization in vivo, indicating that the CRTC-CREB activation is essential for the growth and progression of LKB1-null lung cancer.
evidence: Inferred from the xenograft data showing reduced tumor growth and colonization

claim: The CRTC-CREB activation is essential for the growth and progression of LKB1-null lung cancer.
source: Taken together, these data showed that expression of dnCRTC blocked lung cancer growth and colonization in vivo, indicating that the CRTC-CREB activation is essential for the growth and progression of LKB1-null lung cancer.
evidence: Inferred from the in vivo data showing that blocking CRTC-CREB activation inhibits tumor growth

claim: CRTC activation plays an essential role in the growth of LKB1-deficient lung cancer cells.
source: Our in vitro and in vivo data provide direct evidence that CRTC activation plays an essential role in the growth of LKB1-deficient lung cancer cells and revealed that targeting gain-of-function CREB activation by interfering with the CRTC-CREB interaction is a potential effective strategy in treating LKB1-inactivated lung cancers.
evidence: Inferred from the in vitro and in vivo experimental results

claim: Targeting gain-of-function CREB activation by interfering with the CRTC-CREB interaction is a potential effective strategy in treating LKB1-inactivated lung cancers.
source: Our in vitro and in vivo data provide direct evidence that CRTC activation plays an essential role in the growth of LKB1-deficient lung cancer cells and revealed that targeting gain-of-function CREB activation by interfering with the CRTC-CREB interaction is a potential effective strategy in treating LKB1-inactivated lung cancers.
evidence: Speculative conclusion based on the experimental results

claim: CRTC1 was identified as a fusion partner with the Notch transcriptional co-activator MAML2, due to a t(11;19) chromosomal translocation in mucoepidermoid carcinoma (MEC).
source: We initially identified CRTC1 as a fusion partner with the Notch transcriptional co-activator MAML2, due to a t(11;19) chromosomal translocation in mucoepidermoid carcinoma (MEC), the most common salivary gland malignancies and lung tumors (Tonon et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to the authors' previous publication (Tonon et al., 2003)

claim: The CRTC1-MAML2 fusion binds to CREB via the CRTC1 CBD and potently activates CREB-dependent transcription through its MAML2 TAD.
source: The CRTC1-MAML2 fusion binds to CREB via the CRTC1 CBD and potently activates CREB-dependent transcription through its MAML2 TAD (Wu et al., 2005; Coxon et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2015), which contribute to the fusion's major oncogenic activity (Wu et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Wu et al., 2005; Coxon et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2021)

claim: LKB1-deficiency led to CRTC activation of many CREB-dependent genes, including NR4A2, PTGS2, LYPD3, INSL4, and LINC00473.
source: In our previous studies, we also showed that LKB1-deficiency led to CRTC activation of many CREB-dependent genes, including NR4A2, PTGS2 (aka COX-2), LYPD3, INSL4, and LINC00473, which play important roles in cancer cell growth, survival or invasive properties (Chen et al., 2016; Cao et al., 2015; Gu et al., 2012; Komiya et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to the authors' previous publications (Chen et al., 2016; Cao et al., 2015; Gu et al., 2012; Komiya et al., 2010)

claim: SIKs were the major AMPK family members that mediate LKB1 tumor suppression and SIK knockouts enhanced CRTC target gene expression.
source: Recently, other groups reported that SIKs were the major AMPK family members that mediate LKB1 tumor suppression and SIK knockouts enhanced CRTC target gene expression (Hollstein et al., 2019; Murray et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Hollstein et al., 2019; Murray et al., 2019)

claim: CRTC2 downregulation inhibited the growth of LKB1-deficient NSCLC.
source: Furthermore, CRTC2 downregulation inhibited the growth of LKB1-deficient NSCLC (Rodón et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Rodón et al., 2019)

claim: LKB1-SIK genetic alterations represent a distinct mechanism for the constitutive CRTC-CREB activation that is critical for the tumorigenesis and progression of NSCLC.
source: All these data support a new model that LKB1-SIK genetic alterations represent a distinct mechanism for the constitutive CRTC-CREB activation that is critical for the tumorigenesis and progression of NSCLC.
evidence: Inferred from the collective evidence presented

claim: Upregulation of CRTC1 was observed in response to CRTC2 knockout or CRTC3 knockout, indicating potential functional compensation.
source: We observed complete ablation of endogenous CRTC proteins in their respective knockout cells, as compared to the parental and control knockout cells by western blotting (Figure 2A). Upregulated CRTC1 protein levels were observed in response to CRTC2 knockout or CRTC3 knockout, indicating potential functional compensation.
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A

claim: A recent study reporting CRTC2 shRNA knockdown or knockout in polyclonal cells impaired soft agar formation but did not affect cell proliferation.
source: It should be noted that a recent study reporting CRTC2 shRNA knockdown or knockout in polyclonal cells impaired soft agar formation but did not affect cell proliferation (Rodón et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Rodón et al., 2019)

claim: Two CRTC2 KO single clones only showed minimal inhibition of cell proliferation and soft agar colony formation.
source: In our study, two CRTC2 KO single clones only showed minimal inhibition of cell proliferation and soft agar colony formation; this discrepancy could be explained by the upregulation of CRTC1 in the CRTC2 KO clones.
evidence: Supported by the experimental data from this study

claim: General inhibition of all CRTCs is required for blocking the aberrant CRTC-induced transcriptional program and lung tumorigenesis.
source: Therefore, these data indicate the presence for functional redundancy of the three CRTC co-activator family members in driving aberrant CREB transcriptional program and lung cancer malignant phenotypes, thus suggesting that general inhibition of all CRTCs is required for blocking the aberrant CRTC-induced transcriptional program and lung tumorigenesis.
evidence: Inferred from the functional redundancy observed in individual CRTC knockout experiments

claim: SIK1 is a transcriptional target induced by cAMP-CREB signaling.
source: It should be noted that SIK1 is a transcriptional target induced by cAMP-CREB signaling (Wein et al., 2018) and it was upregulated in LKB1-null cancer cells (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Wein et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2016)

claim: SIK1 downregulation by dnCRTC was only observed in LKB1-null, but not LKB1-wt cancer cells.
source: SIK1 downregulation by dnCRTC was only observed in LKB1-null, but not LKB1-wt cancer cells in this study (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), which is unlikely to have functional consequences as SIK1 kinase is impaired in LKB1-null cancer cells.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: The strategy of blocking the assembly of active CRTC-CREB transcriptional complex and subsequently inhibiting extensive CRTC target genes has the advantage of simultaneously inhibiting multiple deleterious cell signals.
source: The strategy of blocking the assembly of active CRTC-CREB transcriptional complex and subsequently inhibiting extensive CRTC target genes has the advantage of simultaneously inhibiting multiple deleterious cell signals which predicts a greater challenge for resistant cancer cell clones to emerge.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the therapeutic strategy

claim: Inhibition of the CRTC-CREB interaction should reverse the oncogenic activity of CRTC activation.
source: We propose that inhibition of the CRTC-CREB interaction should reverse the oncogenic activity of CRTC activation.
evidence: Speculative proposal based on the experimental findings

claim: Peptides and peptide-like molecules designed to recapitulate a critical interaction motif will have the potential in selectively targeting the CRTC/CREB interaction interface and consequently inhibit lung cancer growth.
source: For instance, peptides and peptide-like molecules designed to recapitulate a critical interaction motif will have the potential in selectively targeting the CRTC/CREB interaction interface and consequently inhibit lung cancer growth.
evidence: Speculative proposal for future therapeutic development

claim: Crystal structural analysis has provided important molecular information of the core CRTC/CREB transcriptional complex.
source: The crystal structural analysis has provided important molecular information of the core CRTC/CREB transcriptional complex (Luo et al., 2012; Song et al., 2018), revealing that CRTC CBD interacts with CREB basic leucine zipper (bZIP) domain forming a 2:2 complex on CRE-containing DNA.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Luo et al., 2012; Song et al., 2018)

claim: CRTC CBD interacts with CREB basic leucine zipper (bZIP) domain forming a 2:2 complex on CRE-containing DNA.
source: The crystal structural analysis has provided important molecular information of the core CRTC/CREB transcriptional complex (Luo et al., 2012; Song et al., 2018), revealing that CRTC CBD interacts with CREB basic leucine zipper (bZIP) domain forming a 2:2 complex on CRE-containing DNA.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Luo et al., 2012; Song et al., 2018)

claim: This study provides direct proof for a critical role of the CRTC-CREB activation in maintaining the malignant phenotypes of LKB1-inactive lung cancers.
source: Collectively, our study provides direct proof for a critical role of the CRTC-CREB activation in maintaining the malignant phenotypes of LKB1-inactive lung cancers and reveals direct inhibition of the CRTC-CREB transcriptional complex via targeting the CRTC-CREB interface as a novel, promising therapeutic approach.
evidence: Inferred from the collective experimental evidence presented in the study

claim: Direct inhibition of the CRTC-CREB transcriptional complex via targeting the CRTC-CREB interface is a novel, promising therapeutic approach.
source: Collectively, our study provides direct proof for a critical role of the CRTC-CREB activation in maintaining the malignant phenotypes of LKB1-inactive lung cancers and reveals direct inhibition of the CRTC-CREB transcriptional complex via targeting the CRTC-CREB interface as a novel, promising therapeutic approach.
evidence: Speculative conclusion based on the experimental results
